title: Decorator Pattern
tagline: Stack behaviours on an object at runtime by wrapping it in a chain of decorators — no subclass explosion, no modification of the original class.

sections.content:
**The Problem:** You need to add behaviours (logging, caching, authentication, compression) to objects dynamically, in different combinations. The naive solution is subclassing: `LoggingUserService extends UserService`, `CachingLoggingUserService extends LoggingUserService`, and so on. With N features you can end up with 2^N subclasses — a combinatorial explosion that is unmanageable and violates the Open/Closed Principle.

**The Decorator pattern** solves this by wrapping an object in a series of thin wrapper objects (decorators), each adding one behaviour. The decorator implements the same interface as the wrapped object, so the caller cannot tell the difference. Behaviours compose by stacking decorators: `new CachingDecorator(new LoggingDecorator(new UserService()))`. Each wrapper adds its layer and delegates to the next.

This is the foundation of **Express/Connect middleware**, **Python decorators**, **Java Spring AOP**, and every HTTP client interceptor chain you have ever used.

sections.caption: FileDataSource is the core component. EncryptionDecorator and CompressionDecorator wrap it — each adds one behaviour while honouring the same DataSource interface.

sections.title: The Coffee Shop Order
sections.content:
You order a plain espresso — that's the **base component**. Add milk: the barista wraps it in a `Milk` decorator that adds cost and a new description. Add caramel: another `Caramel` decorator wraps the result. The cup still behaves like a coffee (same interface), but each wrapper has quietly added its behaviour and its price.

At the register, `getPrice()` unwinds the chain: caramel + milk + espresso. The customer asked for one object; under the hood it's a chain of decorators. You can combine any toppings in any order without needing a `CamelMilkEspresso` class.

**Participants:**

- **Component Interface** — defines the contract that both the real object and all decorators implement. This is what the client depends on.
- **Concrete Component** — the base object with core behaviour (e.g., plain espresso, raw file I/O). It does the real work when no decorator intervenes.
- **Base Decorator** — an abstract class that also implements the Component Interface and holds a reference (`wrappee`) to another Component. Its default implementation simply delegates to the wrappee. This is the key structural piece.
- **Concrete Decorators** — extend Base Decorator. They add behaviour before and/or after calling `super.method()` (which delegates to the wrappee).
- **Client** — assembles the stack by wrapping components in decorators and uses the result through the Component Interface.

**Before vs. After Decoration:**
```
BEFORE: UserService (one flat class with all concerns mixed in)
AFTER:  LoggingDecorator → CachingDecorator → UserService
        (each class has exactly one responsibility; stacked at wiring time)
```

**Decorator vs. Subclassing:** Subclassing adds behaviour at compile time for a specific class. Decoration adds behaviour at runtime for any object that implements the interface — you can decorate third-party classes you cannot subclass.

sections.caption: The call passes through each decorator layer on the way in (adding behaviour) and each result passes back out through the chain — composing without any class knowing about the others.

sections.label: Runtime
sections.explanation: The coffee example shows additive cost/description composition. The service example shows cross-cutting concerns (logging, caching) applied as stackable layers. Notice: switching the stack order `LoggingDecorator(CachingDecorator(UserService()))` would log only cache misses — behaviour changes by reordering, not by modifying any class.

sections.label: Concept
sections.explanation: The nested call `DecoratorB(DecoratorA(...))` shows how each wrapper adds its label around the result. In practice each decorator does meaningful work (encrypt, compress, log, cache) in the same structural position.

sections.content:
**When to use:** Cross-cutting concerns (logging, authentication, caching, rate-limiting, retry logic) that should be applied to some objects but not others, or in varying combinations. Perfect when you cannot modify the original class (library code, third-party SDK).

**When NOT to use:** If the combination of behaviours is always fixed and few, inheritance or a simple composition inside a service is cleaner. Deeply stacked decorators can become hard to debug — stack traces hide which layer introduced a bug.

**In the wild:** Express/Koa middleware chains, Python `@decorator` syntax, Java Spring AOP (`@Transactional`, `@Cacheable`), NestJS guards/interceptors/pipes, and browser `fetch` wrapper libraries that add auth headers, retry, and logging.

items: The **Decorator** pattern adds behaviour to objects at runtime by wrapping them — avoiding the subclass explosion of inheritance-based extension.
All decorators implement the **same interface** as the component they wrap, making them transparent to the client.
Behaviours **compose by nesting**: wrapping order determines execution order — you can change behaviour by reordering decorators, not by editing classes.
Ideal for **cross-cutting concerns** (logging, caching, auth) that need to be applied independently and in combination to different objects.
The cost is **stack depth and debug complexity** — keep decorator stacks shallow and each decorator focused on a single concern.

quiz.question: What problem does the Decorator pattern primarily solve?
options: Providing a simplified interface to a complex subsystem
Adding behaviours to objects dynamically without subclass explosion
Ensuring only one instance of a class exists
Converting one interface to another
quiz.explanation: The Decorator pattern lets you attach behaviours to individual objects at runtime by wrapping them, avoiding the combinatorial explosion of subclasses you would need with inheritance.

quiz.question: Why must a Decorator implement the same interface as the component it wraps?
options: To enable multiple inheritance
So the client can use a decorated object wherever a plain component is expected
To give the decorator access to private fields
To prevent the component from being instantiated directly
quiz.explanation: Implementing the same interface makes the decorator transparent to the client — the client cannot tell whether it is talking to the raw component or a stack of decorators.

quiz.question: You wrap a UserService with LoggingDecorator first, then CachingDecorator. In what order do the behaviours execute on a cache miss?
options: Cache check → Log → UserService.getUser()
Log → Cache check → UserService.getUser()
UserService.getUser() → Cache check → Log
All three execute simultaneously
quiz.explanation: CachingDecorator is the outer wrapper so its code runs first. On a miss it calls into LoggingDecorator, which logs and then calls UserService. The outermost decorator executes first.

quiz.question: How does the Decorator pattern differ from subclassing for adding behaviour?
options: Subclassing works at runtime; decoration works at compile time
Decoration adds behaviour at runtime to any compatible object; subclassing is fixed at compile time for a specific class
Both are equivalent; decoration is just syntactic sugar for subclassing
Subclassing supports multiple behaviours; decoration only supports one
quiz.explanation: Decoration is runtime composition — you can decorate any object that implements the interface, including objects of classes you cannot subclass (third-party, final). Subclassing is a static compile-time relationship tied to a specific parent class.

quiz.question: In the coffee shop example, what does `new WhipDecorator(new MilkDecorator(new Coffee()))` produce when `getCost()` is called?
options: $2.00 (base espresso only)
$2.50 (espresso + milk)
$3.10 (espresso + milk + whip)
$3.85 (espresso + milk + caramel + whip)
quiz.explanation: The chain is: WhipDecorator($0.60) + MilkDecorator($0.50) + Coffee($2.00) = $3.10. Caramel was not added in this stack.

quiz.question: Which real-world framework feature is a direct application of the Decorator pattern?
options: React's virtual DOM diffing
Express middleware pipeline
SQL JOIN clause
CSS box model
quiz.explanation: Express middleware functions wrap each other in a chain — each adds behaviour (auth check, body parsing, logging) and calls `next()` to delegate to the next layer, exactly like decorators.

quiz.question: What is the role of the Base Decorator class?
options: It implements all concrete behaviour so subclasses do not have to
It holds a reference to the wrapped component and delegates by default — concrete decorators override only what they need to change
It prevents any subclass from calling the wrapped component
It replaces the Component Interface entirely
quiz.explanation: The Base Decorator is the structural heart: it stores the wrappee and provides default delegation. Concrete decorators extend it and override methods to add behaviour around the delegation call.

quiz.question: When is the Decorator pattern NOT the best choice?
options: When you need to add logging to one specific class
When behaviours are always applied together and fixed — a simple composition inside a service is cleaner
When you cannot modify a third-party class
When you need to apply caching to multiple different objects
quiz.explanation: If the combination of behaviours is fixed and always the same, a single composed class or service method is simpler and easier to debug than a decorator stack.

quiz.question: What is the key structural difference between a Decorator and an Adapter?
options: A Decorator changes the interface; an Adapter keeps the same interface
An Adapter keeps the same interface; a Decorator adds behaviour while keeping the same interface — but an Adapter translates to a different interface
Both patterns are structurally identical
A Decorator uses inheritance; an Adapter uses composition
quiz.explanation: A Decorator wraps an object to add behaviour, keeping the same interface. An Adapter wraps an object to translate its interface into a different one the client expects. Structure is similar; intent is different.

quiz.question: Why is `super.operation()` (or `this._component.operation()`) the critical call inside a concrete decorator?
options: It prevents the decorator from modifying the result
It delegates to the next layer in the chain — skipping it breaks the delegation and swallows all wrapped behaviour
It initialises the component's state
It enforces the Liskov Substitution Principle
quiz.explanation: The delegation call is what makes the chain work. Without it, the decorator would short-circuit — the base component and any inner decorators would never execute.
